title: Which films need a long slot
prompt: Films of two hours or more need a longer screening slot. Before the scheduling team trusts a model to flag them, they want to see how well it ranks films it never saw. Write `solve(movies)` so it returns the model's area under the ROC curve on its training films and on held-out films.
rules: Use only films with a `runtime_min`, a `release_year` and a `maturity_rating`. The label is 1.0 when `runtime_min` is 120 or more, else 0.0.
Hold out the films whose `F.crc32("movie_id") % 3` is 0; the rest are for training.
Fit a `LogisticRegression` with default settings on the training films only. Its features are the one-hot `maturity_rating` and the `release_year`.
`auc` is the area under the ROC curve from the model's scores, rounded to 3 decimal places. Return two rows, `split` (`train` or `test`), `films` (how many films the split has) and `auc`.
hints: Put `StringIndexer`, `OneHotEncoder`, `VectorAssembler` and `LogisticRegression` in one `Pipeline`, fit it on the training films, and `transform` each split.
`BinaryClassificationEvaluator()` reads `rawPrediction` and `label` and returns the area under the ROC curve by default.
Build the answer with `movies.sparkSession.createDataFrame([...], "split STRING, films BIGINT, auc DOUBLE")`.

from pyspark.sql import functions as F
from pyspark.ml import Pipeline
from pyspark.ml.feature import StringIndexer, OneHotEncoder, VectorAssembler
from pyspark.ml.classification import LogisticRegression
from pyspark.ml.evaluation import BinaryClassificationEvaluator

explanation: Filter the incomplete films, add the label with `F.when(F.col("runtime_min") >= 120, 1.0).otherwise(0.0)`, and split with `F.crc32("movie_id") % 3 == 0` so the same films are held out on every run. The pipeline encodes the maturity rating, adds the year and ends in `LogisticRegression`; fitting it on the training films only keeps the held-out films unseen. `BinaryClassificationEvaluator` scores how well the model ranks long films above short ones: 1.0 is a perfect order, 0.5 is no better than chance. It reads `rawPrediction`, a continuous score; pointing it at the 0/1 `prediction` column throws that ranking away. In the sample the model ranks its six training films much better than the six it never saw, which is the usual pattern on so little data.
